# SYSTEM.md contract — rationale

*Generated by bootstrap-system-md. The header in `SYSTEM.md` states the rules;
this file states why, for humans auditing an agent's edit or disputing one.
Contract: v4 — upgraded 2026-09-02 from the unstamped v3 header (scaffolding
only; no fact lines changed). Replace this line on the next upgrade, don't accrete.*

**Why one file.** Split docs fail by disagreeing: a partial update leaves two
files contradicting each other and no reader can tell which is current. The
orientation tier (what/layout/invariants/env/ledgers) therefore stays in one
file. Reference material (entity lifecycles, UI conventions, surface
catalogs) has low contradiction risk and high volume, so it may extract to
`docs/` with an index left behind.

**Why update-after-change (rule 1).** Documentation maintenance follows a
burst-then-taper pattern when it is a separate task. Making the update a
completion criterion of the change itself, performed by whoever holds the
freshest knowledge, is the only version that survives. Note the honest
limit: this bounds staleness to one round of work, not to zero — the file
is accurate at merge boundaries and can drift mid-round.

**Why integrate-don't-append (rule 2).** Agents honor rule 1 by appending
dated paragraphs, because appending never risks breaking someone else's
prose. The file then grows monotonically as a changelog and a reader must
replay history to learn current behavior. Dates in descriptive sections are
the fingerprint of this failure; the gate greps for them.

**Why log lessons (rule 3).** Gotchas are the highest value-per-line
content: they are the failures that recur across agents and models. They
are cheap to write immediately after paying for them and impossible to
reconstruct later.

**Why ledgers shrink (rule 4).** An append-only ledger without eviction is
just bloat with a nicer name. Deferred items without a trigger are read
every session and acted on never. A gotcha whose cause is now enforced by a
test has done its job — it promotes into the invariants section, where it
is checkable, instead of accumulating.

**Why caps are earned (rule 5).** Raising the size cap when it is hit is
the document-shaped version of re-baselining past a regression. A cap raise
is legal only after a grooming or extraction pass proved the content
incompressible, with a recorded reason.

**Why anchors, not ordinals.** Section numbers get cited from code, configs,
and handoff docs; a grooming pass renumbers; every citation silently points
at the wrong section. Anchors and rule IDs survive; if numbers are used they
are frozen.

**Why invariants name their enforcement point.** A rule with a test is
checkable; a rule alone is a wish. Pinned invariants are the part of the
file that can be trusted without re-reading the code, and the gate can
verify the named test still exists.

**Why the shims.** The dominant failure of a correct file is that nobody
opens it. Root `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md` shims make every auto-loading tool
reach SYSTEM.md without duplicating a single fact.

**Why no secret values.** This file is committed and injected into every
agent's context window. Names and locations only.

## Repo-specific rules and what bought them

These lived in the SYSTEM.md header before the v4 upgrade and moved here so
agents read the rules every session while the reasoning stays auditable.

**Why section numbers are frozen (§1–§13, gaps allowed).** Code, migrations,
and handoff docs cite "§N" from roughly 150 places, and the last renumbering
silently invalidated every one of them. New sections append at the end.
Invariants additionally carry stable ids (`{#inv-slug}`) — cite those from
code in preference to a section number, since they survive any grooming.
Deferred-ledger item numbers are frozen for the same reason: "§11 item N" is
cited from a dozen places, so items append and shipped items are deleted in
place. Priority lives in the item text, not in the ordinal.

**Why two tiers.** The root file is the orientation tier and stays whole.
Pure reference — entity lifecycles (`docs/entities/`) and frontend
conventions (`docs/frontend-conventions.md`) — is extracted, indexed from §4
and §8, and carries this same contract. When the cap is hit, extract more
reference; never split orientation content.

**Why the bold-lead style rule.** Every rule bullet in §6 and in
`docs/entities/` opens with a bolded subject naming what the rule governs,
so the section scans by lead terms — the counter to audience drift.

**Why the header carries no "Prior:" history.** Each header line is replaced,
never accreted; older change history lives in `git log SYSTEM.md`.

**Why the gate's section budget is a share of the cap, not of the total.**
A share-of-total budget tightens every remaining section the moment one is
extracted: after §4 and §8 moved to the reference tier, §6 went from 10% to
20% of the file without a line being added. Against the cap the number
means "lines" and is stable. The budget is 0.25 rather than the template's
0.15 because the orientation tier carries two irreducibly large sections
(§6 invariants, §7 agent surfaces) and the contract forbids splitting
orientation content. Recorded here, not silently widened.

**Why the gate anchors the repo root on its own parent directory.** This
repo is worked in git worktrees under `.claude/worktrees/`; a walk-up search
for SYSTEM.md finds the MAIN checkout's copy from a worktree and silently
validates the wrong file. That happened.

**Why baselines live in `.slopledger.json`.** The migration ledger (§13) is
already mirrored there for the slop ratchet's `ledger_check.py`; one sidecar
for both machine-checked ledgers beats two files that drift apart.
